property_summary: Calls to withdrawAll revert for callers who are not the contract owner (so non-owners cannot make the contract send funds).
Calls to withdrawAll only succeed (do not revert) when invoked by the contract owner; non-owners' calls revert.
If the caller parameter equals this contract's address then withdrawAll must not revert; if it does not equal this contract's address then withdrawAll must revert.
If the input caller equals this contract's address then withdrawAll must not revert; if it does not equal this contract's address then withdrawAll must revert.

For any target address and any value V (0 <= V <= address(this).balance), in the correct contract only the owner can make C send Ether via sendMoney, so after sendMoney(target,V) by a non-owner the contract balance is unchanged; the mutant relaxes onlyOwner allowing outsiders to drain funds, so there exist inputs (a non-owner caller and V>0 to a payable/accepting target) that reduce address(c).balance.

Invariant: Only the owner can cause C to send ETH out so for any non-owner caller and any positive value sent via sendMoney to a callee that accepts funds, the contract balance does not decrease; the mutant that disables the owner check allows a non-owner to withdraw funds, violating this.

Only the owner may cause the contract to transfer out Ether: for every non-owner caller and any positive amount, a call to sendMoney(target, amount) does not decrease address(c).balance when the target is a regular accepting contract; the mutant removing the owner check allows a non-owner to make the contract send funds and thus can decrease address(c).balance for some inputs.

For every non-owner caller and any positive amount sent from C via sendMoney to a callee that reverts on receiving funds, the reference contract will not lose balance because onlyOwner prevents the non-owner from calling sendMoney, while the mutant (onlyOwner always true) allows the non-owner to invoke sendMoney and thus can change address(c).balance for some inputs.

For any callee that reverts when receiving Ether, the reference calls withdraw(address(this).balance) which lets that internal withdraw() (which uses transfer and therefore would revert only if msg.sender cannot receive) be invoked in the contract's context and succeed, while the mutant directly transfer()s to msg.sender and will revert when msg.sender is a contract that rejects Ether — therefore the reference preserves withdrawAll succeeding for all inputs where withdraw would handle transfer differently, but the mutant can fail for some fuzzed amounts and adversarial recipient contracts.

For all callers and deposit amounts, calling withdrawAll() on the correct contract always results in the contract's balance becoming zero (it always successfully forwards the contract balance to the owner via the internal withdraw path), whereas the mutant that uses direct transfer to msg.sender can revert or fail to reduce the contract balance to zero when the owner is a receiver contract that rejects/blocks transfers.

For any fuzzed deposit amount and an owner contract that may reject ETH, the reference C always makes withdrawAll succeed and leaves C's balance zero by delegating to withdraw(address(this).balance), while the mutant that directly transfer()s to msg.sender can fail (revert) or leave balance > 0 when msg.sender is a contract that rejects Ether; the test deploys an adversarial owner contract that rejects receipts to distinguish the implementations.

For any owner address that is a contract which refuses to receive ETH, the reference C's withdrawAll always completes without reverting and leaves C's balance unchanged (because withdraw(address(this).balance) forwards via internal call path that will still behave as contract's withdraw), whereas the mutant that uses payable(msg.sender).transfer(address(this).balance) will revert when msg.sender cannot receive ETH, causing withdrawAll to fail for some inputs.

For any owner address that is a contract implementing a payable fallback/receive, calling withdrawAll after funding C always results in C's balance becoming zero on the correct contract (because it calls withdraw(address(this).balance) which uses the withdraw function path), whereas the mutant that directly does payable(msg.sender).transfer(address(this).balance) can fail to reduce C's balance to zero for some adversarial owner contracts that revert on plain transfer.

For any caller who is the owner and any nonzero amount of Ether held by the contract, calling withdrawAll() transfers the contract's entire balance to the owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) breaks this rule for some inputs.

For any nonzero contract balance and when the caller is owner, calling withdrawAll() makes the contract balance zero (reference calls withdraw(balance)); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero balance and thus violates this rule for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any nonzero initial contract balance provided via fallback, calling withdrawAll() always empties the contract balance (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero balance and thus violates this property for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any nonzero Ether sent into the contract via its fallback, calling withdrawAll() causes the contract balance to decrease by exactly the withdrawn amount (i.e., the reference empties the contract by transferring its full balance to owner), whereas the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave the contract balance unchanged and thus violates this rule for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any nonzero contract balance provided by an external payable fallback (via an adversarial helper that accepts and keeps Ether), calling withdrawAll() on the correct contract transfers all contract balance to the owner (address(c).balance == 0), while the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave the contract balance nonzero; the test fuzzes the deposited amount so the buggy variant fails for some inputs.

For any caller, calling withdrawAll on the reference contract either succeeds for the owner and transfers balance (no revert) or reverts silently for non-owners (require without message) — specifically the reference's withdrawAll never produces a revert with an explicit string payload, while the mutant may revert with the explicit message "NOT_OWNER" for non-owners; therefore the reference never produces a revert that contains the string "NOT_OWNER" but the mutant sometimes does.

For every caller and value, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract either succeeds or reverts without the specific message "NOT_OWNER"; the mutant can revert with the explicit message "NOT_OWNER" for some non-owner callers, so observing whether withdrawAll reverts with that message distinguishes them.

For every caller, calling withdrawAll on the reference C either succeeds or reverts, but it never reverts with the explicit string "NOT_OWNER"; the mutant that tightens onlyOwner to require(msg.sender==owner, "NOT_OWNER") can produce a revert containing "NOT_OWNER" for some non-owner caller, so observing whether withdrawAll reverts with that exact message distinguishes them.

For every caller address and amount, calling withdrawAll on the reference contract never reverts with an explicit revert message string (it either succeeds or reverts without a message); the mutant that tightens onlyOwner to require(..., "NOT_OWNER") can produce an explicit revert message for some non-owner callers, violating that rule.

For every caller, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract never reverts with an explicit revert message string (it either succeeds or reverts silently); the mutant that changes onlyOwner to require(..., "NOT_OWNER") can produce an explicit revert message for some non-owner caller, so observing whether withdrawAll reverts with an explicit message distinguishes them.

For any caller and any sent value, after withdrawAll() completes the correct contract C preserves that depositsCount is unchanged by the external transfer (i.e., depositsCount does NOT increase due to withdrawAll), whereas the mutant increments depositsCount during withdrawAll causing depositsCount to be greater than in the reference for some inputs (re-entrant attacker that increments state during the external transfer).

For any adversarial callee address and any positive balance sent into C, calling withdrawAll by the owner does not increase depositsCount before the contract's balance is forwarded (i.e., after withdrawAll completes depositsCount equals its prior value); the mutant increments depositsCount before forwarding and a reentrant attacker can observe that leading to a higher depositsCount after completion.

For every caller and any balance, when the owner calls withdrawAll, the contract's depositsCount does not increase (remains equal to its prior value); the mutant increments depositsCount during withdrawAll causing depositsCount to be larger after completion for some adversarial reentrant callee.

For every caller and any admissible attacker contract and Ether balance, when the owner calls withdrawAll the depositsCount remains equal to its prior value after the call (no increment happens inside withdrawAll); the mutant increments depositsCount inside withdrawAll so a reentrant attacker can observe a larger depositsCount after completion.

For any attacker contract and any prior depositsCount, when the owner calls withdrawAll the final depositsCount equals the prior depositsCount plus any increments caused by external fallback calls during the withdrawal (i.e. withdrawAll itself does not unconditionally increment depositsCount before the external call); the mutant violates this by unconditionally incrementing depositsCount inside withdrawAll, causing final depositsCount to be strictly greater than the reference for some fuzzed initial balance and attacker behavior.
Only the contract owner can withdraw all contract balance (withdrawAll succeeds for owner and would revert for non-owner callers).
Calling withdraw(...) should succeed for the contract owner (the account that deployed C) and revert for non-owner callers.
Only a caller whose address equals C.owner (the deployer) can successfully call withdraw; in particular if msg.sender equals the owner, withdraw must not revert.
If the caller of run is the same as tx.origin (i.e., not called via a contract) then calling withdraw(...) must not revert for the true owner of C.
If the caller of run equals the contract C.owner (as returned by its public getter), then calling withdraw(...) must not revert.

For every caller and amount, only the contract owner (the deployer) can cause ether to be withdrawn from the contract via withdraw/sendMoney; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead of msg.sender allows a contract-mediated call (where tx.origin is owner but msg.sender is an intermediate contract) to withdraw funds, violating the rule for some caller/attacker addresses.

Only the deployer (owner) can cause withdrawals from C when calling sendMoney; the mutant that uses tx.origin allows an intermediate malicious contract (where tx.origin == owner but msg.sender != owner) to withdraw, so there exist inputs (an intermediate attacker contract address and a nonzero amount) that make the mutant change contract balance while the reference never does.

For all target addresses and amounts, only the deployer (owner) can cause C's balance to decrease via sendMoney; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead of msg.sender allows an intermediate contract (where tx.origin == owner but msg.sender != owner) to withdraw funds, so there exist inputs (an attacker contract address and nonzero amount) that make the mutant reduce address(c).balance while the reference never does.

For any target contract address and nonzero value, calling sendMoney(target, value) from any caller that is not the owner must never reduce C's balance (only the owner can cause balance to decrease); the mutant that checks tx.origin instead of msg.sender allows an intermediate malicious contract (where tx.origin == owner but msg.sender != owner) to make C send funds, violating this rule for some inputs.

For every target address and amount, if a non-owner contract calls sendMoney on C then C's balance must not decrease (only direct calls from owner may move funds); the mutant that uses tx.origin allows a malicious intermediary contract (where tx.origin == owner but msg.sender != owner) to withdraw funds, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(amount) the contract's balance decreases by exactly the requested amount and correspondingly the owner's received ETH increases by that amount; the mutant that sends amount/2 violates this because the contract balance does not drop by the full requested amount for some amounts.

For any owner withdraw amount > 0 that is <= contract balance, calling withdraw(amount) transfers exactly that amount out (so address(c).balance decreases by amount); the mutant that halves the transfer breaks this for some amounts.

For any owner and any nonzero withdraw amount that does not exceed the contract balance, calling withdraw(amount) succeeds and results in address(c).balance decreasing by exactly amount; the mutant that halves the transferred value breaks this because the balance will decrease by only amount/2 for some amounts.

For any owner and any nonzero amount <= contract balance, after calling withdraw(amount) the caller's received ETH increase equals the amount withdrawn (so address(c).balance decreases by exactly amount); the mutant that sends only amount/2 violates this for some amounts.

For any owner and any nonzero withdraw amount that is exactly 1 wei, calling withdraw(1) transfers exactly 1 wei out (contract balance decreases by 1); the mutant that halves transfers will send 0 for this amount and thus violates the rule for some input.

For any caller who is owner and any amount <= contract balance, calling withdraw succeeds in transferring that amount out (reducing contract balance accordingly); the mutant that replaces transfer with a non-reverting low-level call can fail to send funds when the recipient reverts, leaving the contract balance unchanged.

For any recipient that may revert on receiving Ether, the correct contract's withdraw will always reduce the contract balance by the withdrawn amount (because transfer reverts on failure), whereas the mutant using call that ignores success can leave the contract balance unchanged when the recipient reverts.

For any owner-initiated withdraw(amount) where the recipient reverts when receiving Ether, the reference contract always reverts (so address(c).balance decreases only when transfer succeeds) but the mutant using unchecked call may silently leave address(c).balance unchanged — thus the reference never preserves its balance on such failing recipients while the mutant can.

For any owner-initiated withdraw(amount) where the recipient's fallback reverts, the reference contract (which uses transfer) will revert the withdraw call (so the call does not succeed), while the mutant that uses call and ignores success will return (not revert) leaving the contract balance unchanged; thus the general rule: withdraw to a reverting recipient always reverts (no successful call) in the reference, but the mutant permits a successful return despite not sending funds.
